q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Rank by atomic number of the attached atoms; for the two carbons, list what each one is bonded to (a double bond counts its partner twice).
w: Cl (Z = 17) is first. The vinyl carbon carries (C, C, H) because the C=C partner is duplicated, which beats CH3 (H, H, H). H is last. Viewing with H pointed away from you, Cl → CH=CH2 → CH3 runs clockwise, so carbon a is R.
x: The priority order is right, but the direction was read with H toward the viewer without reversing it; correctly viewed, the path is clockwise (R).
CH<sub>3</sub> (H, H, H) cannot outrank the vinyl carbon (C, C, H); the duplicated C from the double bond wins the first point of difference.
CH<sub>3</sub> does not outrank CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, and with that wrong order the path would also be read as S, not R.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Compare the two carbon branches one atom at a time. The first point of difference decides; you never jump ahead to the double bond.
w: OH is first. Next compare the atoms attached to carbon a: the isopropyl CH carries (C, C, H) and the allyl CH2 carries (C, H, H). The first point of difference already favors isopropyl, so the C=C further out never matters. With H pointing away, OH → CH(CH3)2 → CH2CH=CH2 runs counterclockwise: S.
x: This ranks the allyl group above isopropyl because of its double bond, but the double bond is two atoms out; at the first atom isopropyl (C, C, H) beats CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H).
The priority order is right, but the direction is reversed; with H pointing away the path is counterclockwise.
The allyl group does not outrank isopropyl, so this order is wrong even though the letter matches.

q: Carbon a carries no hydrogen. What is its configuration?
c: It is not a chirality center, because it has no hydrogen
It cannot be assigned until the sign of optical rotation is measured
h: A chirality center needs four different groups, not a hydrogen. Here the lowest-priority group is a carbon group.
w: Carbon a has four different groups: OH, CH=CH2, CH2CH3 and CH3. Priorities: OH > CH=CH2 (C, C, H) > CH2CH3 (C, H, H) > CH3 (H, H, H). With the CH3 (priority 4) pointing away, OH → vinyl → ethyl runs counterclockwise, so the center is S.
x: R comes from reading the circle with the methyl (lowest priority) toward you without reversing, or from ranking ethyl above vinyl.
A chirality center needs four different groups, not an H; this carbon has OH, vinyl, ethyl and methyl.
R/S comes from the CIP rules and the 3-D arrangement; it has no fixed relation to the sign of rotation.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a of this 2-methylcyclohexanone, and which priority order supports it?
h: Treat the two ring directions as two different substituents and list the atoms attached to each neighbor of carbon a.
w: The carbonyl carbon carries (O, O, C) because the C=O oxygen is duplicated; the ring CH2 carries (C, H, H); CH3 carries (H, H, H). So C=O > ring CH2 > CH3 > H. With H pointing away, the path runs counterclockwise: S.
x: The priorities are right but the direction is reversed; check whether H is toward or away from you before reading the circle.
CH<sub>3</sub> (H, H, H) loses to the ring CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H) at the first point of difference.
The carbonyl carbon (O, O, C) outranks the ring CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H), so this order is wrong even though the letter matches.

q: Assign the configurations of carbons a and b.
h: At each center the heteroatom is first, and the neighboring ring carbon that carries the other heteroatom is second.
w: At a: NH2 > Cb (O, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H; the path is clockwise with H away, so a is R. At b: OH > Ca (N, C, H) > ring CH2 > H; also clockwise, so b is R. The answer is a = R, b = R (the trans isomer).
x: This is the enantiomer; both directions were read with H toward the viewer without reversing.
Carbon b was misread; at b the OH is first and Ca (N, C, H) is second, which gives R.
Carbon a was misread; at a the NH2 is first and Cb (O, C, H) is second, which gives R.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Write the three attached atoms for each carbon branch. One oxygen beats any number of carbons at the first point of difference.
w: The attached sets are CH2OH (O, H, H), C≡CH (C, C, C, the triple bond duplicated twice) and CH(CH3)2 (C, C, H). Compare highest atoms first: O beats C, so CH2OH is first; then (C, C, C) beats (C, C, H). Order: CH2OH > C≡CH > CH(CH3)2 > H. With H pointing away the path is counterclockwise, so S.
x: C≡CH has more attached atoms, but CIP compares the highest atom first: the O on CH<sub>2</sub>OH beats every C.
Group size or mass does not set priority; isopropyl (C, C, H) is last among the three carbon groups.
With C≡CH ranked first the circle would read R, so this combination is internally inconsistent as well as misranked.

q: Carbon a in this labeled ethanol carries one H and one deuterium (D = 2H). What is its configuration?
c: Not a chirality center, because H and D are the same element
h: When atomic numbers tie, the CIP rules use atomic mass. Then ask where D ranks relative to a carbon.
w: Isotopes are different groups: D (mass 2) outranks H (mass 1), but both rank below carbon. Priorities: OH > CH3 > D > H. With H pointing away, OH → CH3 → D is clockwise, so the center is R. Compounds like this are chiral and are used to follow the stereochemistry of reactions.
x: The priority order is right but the direction is reversed; read the path with H away from you.
D has atomic number 1, so it ranks below carbon (Z = 6); mass only breaks ties between the same element.
H and D differ in mass, which the CIP rules use to break the tie, so carbon a has four different groups.

q: The natural (L) form of the amino acid cysteine is drawn. What is the configuration at carbon a?
c: S, because every L amino acid is S
h: Compare the first atoms attached to the two carbon branches: CH<sub>2</sub>SH has (S, H, H) and CO<sub>2</sub>H has (O, O, O).
w: NH2 is first. CH2SH (S, H, H) beats CO2H (O, O, O) because S (Z = 16) beats O (Z = 8) at the first point of difference. The order NH2 > CH2SH > CO2H > H gives clockwise with H away, so L-cysteine is R. It is the common exception to "L = S".
x: D/L is a Fischer-projection label and R/S is a CIP label; they usually line up for amino acids but not for cysteine, where sulfur changes the priorities.
CO<sub>2</sub>H has three oxygens, but CIP compares the highest atom first, and one S beats any O.
If CO<sub>2</sub>H did outrank CH<sub>2</sub>SH, this drawing would be S, so the reason and the letter do not fit together.

h: Number from the end nearer the OH (C2 carries OH, C3 carries Cl), then assign each center separately.
w: At C2: OH > C3 (Cl, C, H) > CH3 > H. At C3: Cl > C2 (O, C, H) > CH3 > H. Only one structure gives S at the OH carbon and R at the Cl carbon, so it is (2S,3R). The other three are its enantiomer (2R,3S) and the two diastereomers (2S,3S) and (2R,3R).
x: This is (2R,3S), the enantiomer: both centers are inverted.
This is (2S,3S); the OH carbon is right but the Cl carbon is S.
This is (2R,3R); the Cl carbon is right but the OH carbon is R.

q: Rank these substituents in CIP priority, highest first: −CO<sub>2</sub>H, −CHO, −CH<sub>2</sub>OH, −CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
h: Write the set of three atoms on each attached carbon (count a double-bonded O twice) and compare highest atom first.
w: Attached sets: CO2H (O, O, O); CHO (O, O, H); CH2OH (O, H, H); CH(CH3)2 (C, C, H). All three oxygen-bearing carbons start with O, so compare the next atom; the isopropyl group loses at the first atom. Order: −CO2H > −CHO > −CH2OH > −CH(CH3)2.
x: CHO has (O, O, H) and CO<sub>2</sub>H has (O, O, O); the third atom decides, and O beats H.
CH<sub>2</sub>OH has an O on its first carbon, which beats the (C, C, H) of isopropyl regardless of how many carbons follow.
Size and mass do not set priority; isopropyl has no O on its first carbon, so it is last.

q: What is the relationship between compounds I and II?
h: Assign R/S to both centers of each compound and compare: are both inverted, one inverted, or none?
w: Both are 3-chlorobutan-2-ol, so they are stereoisomers. I is (2R,3R) and II is (2S,3R): the OH carbon differs and the Cl carbon is the same. Stereoisomers that differ at some but not all centers are diastereomers.
x: Enantiomers differ at every chirality center; here the Cl-bearing carbon is R in both.
The OH-bearing carbon is R in I and S in II, so they are not the same compound.
The atoms are connected in the same order in both (OH on C2, Cl on C3), so they are not constitutional isomers.

q: Compounds I and II are both 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol. What is their relationship?
h: Do not judge by the orientation on the page. Assign R/S at the OH carbon and at the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon of each.
w: In both drawings the OH carbon is R (OH > C–CH3 ring carbon > ring CH2 > H) and the CH3 carbon is R. Same configuration at every center means the drawings are the same molecule turned on the page: identical (both are the trans isomer, (1R,2R)).
x: Enantiomers would show opposite configurations at both centers; here both centers match.
Diastereomers would differ at exactly one of the two centers; neither center differs.
Both have OH and CH<sub>3</sub> on adjacent ring carbons, so the connectivity is the same.

q: What is the relationship between drawings I and II of 2,3-dibromobutane?
h: Assign both centers in each drawing. If a molecule has R and S at two equivalently substituted centers, ask what its mirror image is.
w: Each drawing has one R and one S center. For 2,3-dibromobutane, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same molecule because the two halves are equivalent and an internal mirror plane exists. Both drawings are the meso compound, so they are identical.
x: A meso compound is its own mirror image, so it has no enantiomer; the mirror-image look of the drawings is misleading.
Diastereomers would differ at only one center, but here (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) describe the same achiral molecule.
The two drawings are identical, but each has one R and one S center, so neither is (2R,3R).

q: What is the relationship between compounds I and II?
h: Decide cis or trans first. Only the cis isomer has an internal mirror plane.
w: Both are trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane (one Br wedged, one dashed). I is (1R,2R) and II is (1S,2S). Trans-1,2-disubstitution with identical groups has no mirror plane, so the molecule is chiral and I and II are enantiomers.
x: Only the cis isomer of 1,2-dibromocyclopentane is meso; the trans isomer has no internal mirror plane.
Both are trans with opposite configurations at both centers, which makes them mirror images, not diastereomers.
Both have Br on adjacent ring carbons, so the connectivity is the same.

q: Menthol (peppermint) has three chirality centers. Assign carbons a, b and c.
h: At each ring carbon, the two ring directions are different groups: follow each until they differ.
w: a (C–OH): OH > ring C bearing the isopropyl (C, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H → R. b (C–isopropyl): Ca (O, C, H) > isopropyl CH (C, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H → S. c (C–CH3): both ring neighbors are CH2 (C, H, H) and tie; one atom further, the path toward Ca reaches a carbon bearing O, which beats the CH2 on the other path. So ring path toward a > other ring path > CH3 > H → R. Natural menthol is (1R,2S,5R): a = R, b = S, c = R.
x: This is the enantiomer (all three inverted), which comes from reading every center with H toward you without reversing.
At b, Ca (with its O) outranks the isopropyl carbon (C, C, H); swapping them gives the wrong letter R.
At a, OH is first and the isopropyl-bearing ring carbon is second; that order gives R, not S.

q: Which of the tagged carbons is a chirality center (four different groups)?
h: For each ring carbon, compare the two paths around the ring. If they are identical, that carbon has two identical groups.
w: Carbon a carries H, CH3, CH2CH3 and the cyclohexyl ring: four different groups, so it is a chirality center. Carbons b and c sit at C1 and C4 of a 1,4-disubstituted ring; the two ring paths from each are identical, so neither is a chirality center (they do make cis/trans isomers possible, but cis and trans here are achiral diastereomers). Carbon d is a CH2. a only.
x: Carbons b and c each have two identical ring paths (C1 and C4 of the ring), so they lack four different groups.
Being able to show cis/trans isomerism does not make b and c chirality centers; each still has two identical ring branches.
Carbon d is a CH2 with two hydrogens, so it cannot be a chirality center.

q: A wedge-and-dash drawing shows one chirality center. Which operation on the drawing turns it into a drawing of the enantiomer?
c: Exchange the positions of two groups on the chirality center
Rotate the whole drawing 180° in the plane of the page
Make two separate exchanges of groups on the chirality center
Rotate the whole drawing 90° in the plane of the page
h: Which of these changes is a real motion of a molecule, and which one breaks and remakes bonds?
w: Any single exchange of two groups inverts a center: one swap gives the enantiomer, a second swap restores the original. Rotating a wedge-and-dash drawing in the page is just moving the molecule, so it leaves the configuration unchanged at any angle.
x: Rotating a molecule never changes its configuration; the wedges stay wedges and the dashes stay dashes.
Two exchanges invert the center twice, which returns the original configuration.
A 90° turn inverts a Fischer projection, but a wedge-and-dash drawing is a true 3-D picture, so it can be turned in the page by any angle without change.

q: (2R,3R)-2,3-Dibromopentane has [α]D = +x. What can be said about [α]D of (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromopentane?
c: It cannot be predicted; it must be measured
It is 0, because the compound is meso
h: Decide first how the two compounds are related, then recall which relationship fixes the rotation.
w: Changing one of two centers gives a diastereomer, and diastereomers have unrelated physical properties, including optical rotation; the value must be measured. Only the enantiomer, (2S,3S), is required to show −x. 2,3-Dibromopentane has different groups (CH3 and CH2CH3) on its two ends, so no stereoisomer is meso.
x: −x belongs to the enantiomer (2S,3S), where both centers are inverted.
Meso needs equivalent halves; with CH<sub>3</sub> on one end and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the other, (2R,3S) is chiral.
Diastereomers are different compounds, so there is no reason for their rotations to match.
